title: Isolation
description: Choose an explicit transaction observation contract, compare snapshots and locking reads, and protect current and cross-row decisions without overstating isolation guarantees.

questions.question_text: What does the transaction isolation contract specify?
options: Every query physically runs alone
Which concurrent interactions and observations are permitted under the chosen level and engine
Every application input is correct
All copies immediately have identical values
questions.explanation: Weaker levels can permit anomalies, including dirty reads at READ UNCOMMITTED. Do not make an unqualified no-intermediate-state promise.

questions.question_text: Without isolation, what problem could occur if T2 reads while T1 is mid-update?
options: T2 would always see a clean, fully consistent snapshot
T2 could see a confusing mix of some already-updated and some not-yet-updated rows, a state that never really existed
T2 would be blocked from reading entirely
T1 would automatically pause until T2 finishes
questions.explanation: An insufficient observation contract can expose a mix that never existed as one committed state; precise behavior depends on the engine, read type and level.

questions.question_text: Does serializable behavior require literally executing every whole transaction one at a time?
options: Yes, all independent work must always wait
No; eligible work can interleave while preserving required serial equivalence, though coordination has workload-dependent costs
Only on a single table
Only for read-only queries
questions.explanation: Serial and serializable are distinct. Stronger guarantees can require blocking or retries without global physical serialization.

questions.question_text: How do real database systems typically balance isolation strength against performance?
options: They always use perfect (fully serial) isolation
They offer configurable isolation levels (Chapter 25) that trade some isolation strength for better throughput
They disable isolation entirely by default
Isolation cannot be configured in any real system
questions.explanation: Levels provide different contracts. Performance effects depend on workload, plans, contention and implementation, rather than a universal weaker-is-faster guarantee.

questions.question_text: Is Isolation the same concern as Atomicity?
options: Yes, they are synonyms
Atomicity concerns supported all-or-nothing completion; isolation specifies permitted concurrent observations under the chosen level and engine.
Isolation only applies to single-statement transactions
Atomicity is a stricter version of Isolation
questions.explanation: Atomicity concerns one supported transaction outcome; isolation concerns concurrent interactions and observations under the selected contract.

questions.question_text: What kinds of anomalies does Isolation (at varying strength) aim to prevent?
options: Syntax errors
Concurrency anomalies like dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads (Chapter 23)
Disk space exhaustion
Slow query performance
questions.explanation: Isolation levels are specifically calibrated against these named concurrency anomalies.

questions.question_text: Does 'isolation' in ACID refer to operating-system process isolation?
options: Yes, they are the same concept
No — ACID Isolation is specifically about transaction visibility rules within the database, unrelated to OS/container isolation
ACID Isolation is implemented using OS process isolation exclusively
This is an interchangeable term across all contexts
questions.explanation: Despite the shared word, these are unrelated concepts in different domains.

questions.question_text: At a documented serializable contract, how should supported concurrent results relate to a serial reference?
options: All levels allow every dirty read
They should be equivalent to some permitted serial execution under the engine model
Every transaction must start at the same instant
The result must maximize every balance
questions.explanation: This is a serializable-level statement, not a promise that every weaker isolation level looks as though no other transaction exists.

questions.question_text: Does transactional support alone prove serializable execution for every query?
options: No
Yes, every level is serializable
Only with a primary key
Only for text tables
questions.explanation: The actual isolation level and statement semantics determine the contract.

questions.question_text: Does an older committed snapshot value necessarily constitute a dirty read?
options: Yes, all old data is dirty
No
Only if numeric
Only after an UPDATE
questions.explanation: Dirty reads concern an uncommitted source, not age alone.

questions.question_text: Can serializable work physically interleave?
options: No, one transaction must always occupy the whole server
Yes, if required serial equivalence is preserved
Only if all work aborts
Only if no rows exist
questions.explanation: Serializability is an equivalence guarantee, not literal no-overlap scheduling.

questions.question_text: What does ordinary InnoDB READ COMMITTED generally provide per statement?
options: One permanent database-wide snapshot
Every uncommitted writer value
A fresh committed snapshot
Only replica values
questions.explanation: Later statements can observe newly committed changes.

questions.question_text: What generally establishes the ordinary REPEATABLE READ snapshot in this context?
options: A comment before BEGIN
Any other connection’s query
The table filename
The first consistent read
questions.explanation: First-read timing matters for snapshot contents.

questions.question_text: Does a stable snapshot automatically enforce a cross-row on-call invariant?
options: No
Yes, any snapshot is sufficient
Only if names are unique
Only if both rows are integers
questions.explanation: Decision coordination must protect the actual shared rule.

questions.question_text: What must a reservation inspect after a conditional decrement?
options: Only whether SQL parsed
Whether the required row effect occurred
Only its output color
Only the number of comments
questions.explanation: An unmet predicate can return no changed row without an SQL exception.

questions.question_text: Do locking reads and ordinary consistent reads necessarily share one visibility context?
options: Yes, for every statement
Only with SELECT star
No
Only if sorted
questions.explanation: InnoDB current locking reads differ from ordinary historical snapshot reads.

questions.question_text: What should a retryable aborted operation normally recompute?
options: Only a stale replacement value
Only an external email
The old snapshot identity
Its complete logical decision with fresh state
questions.explanation: Earlier observations may no longer be valid for the new attempt.

questions.question_text: Can weaker isolation be declared universally faster?
options: No
Yes, for every workload
Only for three columns
Only after a restart
questions.explanation: Plans, contention and transaction duration also determine performance.

questions.question_text: Why inspect every writer of a shared invariant?
options: Only screens can modify data
An alternate path can bypass one workflow’s coordination
Background imports inherit every UI rule
All writers automatically serialize
questions.explanation: Correctness must hold at the trusted shared boundary.

questions.question_text: What does a one-session SELECT result not prove?
options: The returned literal value
The output column name
Actual multi-connection isolation behavior
That the query executed
questions.explanation: Interleaving, waits and outcomes require controlled concurrent evidence.

original_questions.question_text: From a single transaction's own point of view under proper isolation, how does concurrent execution appear?
options: As if many other transactions are visibly interleaved with it
As if it were running alone, even though other transactions may be executing concurrently
As a series of random errors
Isolation provides no particular appearance guarantee
original_questions.explanation: This 'as if alone' illusion is exactly what isolation aims to provide to each transaction.

notes:
## Specify what concurrent work is allowed to observe

Isolation describes the interaction and observation contract between concurrent transactions. At a strong serializable level, supported executions should have results equivalent to some serial transaction order under the engine's documented model. Weaker levels permit different anomalies. Saying a database supports transactions therefore does not establish that every request behaves as though no other request exists, or that every SELECT is prevented from seeing every kind of intermediate state.

Start with the decision a workflow must make. A historical report can need a consistent view of a past committed state. A live dashboard can prefer a fresh committed observation on each statement. A last-seat reservation must connect a current availability decision with the write that consumes the seat. These purposes involve different observations and enforcement requirements even when all use the same tables and familiar transaction commands.

## Separate isolation from atomicity

Atomicity concerns one transaction's supported commit outcome: its participating pending changes do not remain as an arbitrary partially committed transaction after abort. Isolation concerns how another transaction interacts with that work while executions overlap. A writer reading its own pending changes is not proof that other transactions can read them, and another reader seeing an old committed version is not proof that the writer performed no update.

Consider moving three kits from depot one to depot two. Within the writer's transaction the source can already be changed while the destination is not yet changed. Its own code must understand that pending state. A competing operation's permitted observation depends on isolation and statement type. Preventing partial transaction commit and preventing a particular intermediate observation are related reliability concerns with distinct definitions and tests.

## Identify anomalies through complete histories

A dirty read consumes another transaction's uncommitted value. The writer might later commit or roll back; the read is dirty at the time it occurs. A nonrepeatable read observes different committed values for the same item across reads in one transaction. A phantom concerns a changed set of qualifying rows. These names classify particular observations, not a universal ranking of business severity.

A lost update can arise when two clients read the same committed quantity and later send unconditional replacement values computed from that stale observation. No dirty read is necessary for one intended decrement to disappear. Write skew can involve different rows: each transaction checks a shared invariant and changes a different part, allowing their combined effect to violate the rule. Analyze the actual reads, predicates, writes and outcomes instead of choosing a label from final row values alone.

| Concern | Question to ask | Evidence needed |
|---|---|---|
| Dirty read | Was the source writer committed when read? | Actual observed version and writer outcome |
| Nonrepeatable read | Did one reader see a changed committed item? | Both reads and intervening commit |
| Lost update | Was an intended effect overwritten? | Operation contract and stale-write history |
| Write skew | Did separate decisions violate a shared invariant? | Cross-row reads, predicates and final effects |

## Understand committed snapshots

InnoDB ordinary consistent reads can use multiversion data rather than block behind every current writer. Under READ COMMITTED, each such statement obtains a fresh committed snapshot. Under REPEATABLE READ, the first ordinary consistent read generally establishes the snapshot used by later ordinary consistent reads in that transaction. The timing of that first read therefore matters, not merely the time the client issued START TRANSACTION.

A stable snapshot can keep a report internally repeatable while another transaction commits changes. It does not mean every statement inside the transaction reads only that historical view. Own writes and locking reads have different behavior. Combining an earlier snapshot observation with a later current locking read requires care because the observations can refer to different database moments. State which read type each part of the workflow uses.

## Use current protection for a current decision

A suitable conditional relative update can connect an eligibility predicate to a quantity change in one statement. A locking read inside a transaction can protect a row while the caller makes a dependent decision. Neither should be chosen mechanically: the complete invariant can involve additional rows or a range whose absence matters. An appropriate index and predicate influence which records and intervals an engine actually protects.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT remaining FROM isolation_seats
WHERE session_id=7 FOR UPDATE;
-- Trusted workflow validates the protected state and request.
UPDATE isolation_seats SET remaining=remaining-1
WHERE session_id=7 AND remaining>0;
-- Trusted workflow verifies the required effect.
COMMIT;
```

This fragment assumes a disposable InnoDB fixture and one authorized reservation attempt. It names required application decisions without implementing them in comments. If the predicate matches no row, statement success is not a successful reservation. If another condition spans several sessions, locking only session seven might not protect that broader rule. The transaction boundary and coordination mechanism must follow the real business requirement.

## Compare stronger and weaker contracts honestly

READ UNCOMMITTED can permit dirty reads in InnoDB. READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ prevent that particular anomaly for ordinary reads under their contracts while differing in snapshot behavior and other interactions. SERIALIZABLE aims for a stronger serial-equivalence guarantee and can introduce locking, blocking or retries depending on context. Named levels must be interpreted through the actual engine rather than assumed identical across every database.

Stronger coordination can increase resource use or contention for a workload, but there is no universal rule that a weaker level always makes every query faster. An inefficient plan, long transaction or hot row can dominate latency at several levels. Conversely, blindly serializing all transactions globally can waste independent execution opportunities. Measure the intended workload while preserving its correctness requirement instead of treating performance and isolation as one fixed slider.

Serializable execution also does not require literally running one transaction at a time. Eligible work can interleave while the engine preserves the required serial-equivalent behavior. This distinction is why a serial reference model helps correctness reasoning without forcing every implementation to use a single global application lock. Inspect actual guarantees and failure handling rather than equating physical overlap with an automatic isolation violation.

## Protect invariants beyond one row

Suppose two coordinators are on call and at least one must remain. Each transaction reads that another coordinator is available and turns its own row off. Stable snapshots of the original state do not by themselves prove the combined rule survives. A shared guard row followed by every relevant decision path, or another verified serializable strategy, can coordinate this cross-row invariant. One counter update or unique row key alone does not express that rule.

The repair must include all writers, not just the visible screen. An administrative tool or background import using another path can bypass application-only coordination. Test allowed and denied outcomes at the trusted enforcement boundary, including conflicting attempts and cleanup. A user interface warning can explain contention but cannot establish that a direct caller is prevented from violating the shared invariant.

## Handle aborts and connection lifetime

An isolation conflict can lead to waiting, timeout or transaction abort rather than the exact interleaving imagined in a textbook. Retry the complete logical operation when the documented error is retryable, using fresh observations and bounded attempts. Repeating only a stale final assignment can preserve the original mistake. A lost commit acknowledgment also requires reconciliation rather than blind repetition of a potentially completed effect.

Pooled sessions can retain isolation settings or unresolved transactions unless the driver and application deliberately reset them. End the intended transaction on every path and discard an unusable connection when cleanup cannot be confirmed. A transaction that only reads can still retain a snapshot or other resources. Inspect session state and connection ownership instead of assuming that no visible write means no cleanup responsibility.

## Solve two isolation design exercises

First exercise: A reads a value under READ COMMITTED, B changes it and commits, and A reads again. Predict the new committed observation. Repeat under an already established ordinary REPEATABLE READ snapshot and predict the earlier value instead. Explain why neither ordinary committed read needs to expose B's unfinished version. Record both connections and exact barriers rather than using a screenshot as the entire proof.

Second exercise: two requests each observe one remaining seat. Describe a conditional update or protected decision that allows at most one reservation, then include the zero-row denial and rollback branches. Extend the requirement to two related rows and identify what additional coordination is needed. Continue with [isolation-level experiments](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/isolation-level-lab), [locking protocols](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/locking-protocol-lab) and [serial schedules](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/serial-schedule) to connect the observation contract with a testable operation.

diagrams.caption: Stable observations and protected decisions answer different questions
diagrams.description: A historical snapshot can remain stable while a writer commits. A current locking decision protects relevant resources. Serializable behavior targets serial equivalence without requiring literal global one-at-a-time execution.
